abstract: Computer use has reached a turning point: the focus is expanding from GUI-only interaction to systems that complete tasks on users’ computers through visual and programmatic interfaces. We define a generalist computer-use agent (GCUA) as a system in which the model chooses how to observe, act, and organize its work across visual and programmatic interfaces. Yet frontier implementations, such as GPT-6 Astra’s computer-use system, remain largely closed, limiting systematic study of their design. We introduce Open Generalist CUA (OpenGCUA), an ongoing project to develop and open the full stack for GCUAs with the community. This report presents the first release of Open Generalist CUA. Code execution is a key feature of our agent design: it lets intermediate results determine subsequent operations and enables models to apply their existing programming capabilities directly to computer interaction. We also propose harness-to-model decision transfer, moving selected observations and task-state decisions from fixed harness rules to the model. On OSWorld-v2, our full configuration improves task scores across all eight evaluated models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5, raising mean partial score by +19.6 points and reducing reported steps per task by an average of 53.0% relative to batched GUI-only execution. We release our implementation and prompts, evaluation trajectories from all eight models, and preliminary versions of a real-device harness and a cross-device SDK. The harness addresses real-device challenges not fully captured by benchmarks, while the SDK provides a common programming interface across computers, mobiles and browsers. Across four real macOS tasks under our real-device harness, selected Qwen3.8-Max runs use 19.4 times as many reported reasoning tokens as GPT-6 Astra, highlighting substantial differences between models in real-device execution efficiency.

sections.body: The introduction defines a generalist computer-use agent as a system that completes computer tasks through both visual interaction and programmatic access, with the model choosing how to observe, act and organize its work. It argues that frontier systems such as GPT-6 Astra remain largely closed, which limits study of their design. The first release covers agent design and evaluation, trajectories from frontier models, and preliminary versions of a real-device harness and a cross-device SDK. The release does not include a trained model. The stated contributions include a 19.6 point gain in mean partial score across eight models and a 19.4 times difference in reasoning tokens on four real macOS tasks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Open Generalist computer-use agent project releases agent designs, evaluation trajectories and preliminary tools, without a trained model.

sections.body: The section defines a generalist agent by the decisions it makes at each step, not by the components it contains. At each step the model chooses which views to request, such as a screenshot or an accessibility tree, writes a program over graphical, accessibility, shell and API primitives, and updates its working state. The authors formalize this as a policy and note that a GUI+CLI agent such as Qwen-UI-Agent fixes a screenshot view and a harness rule for memory. Table 1 compares agent families on these three decisions. The text notes that having all five layers does not mean an agent chooses well between interfaces.
sections.heading: Generalist CUA: Definition and Positioning
sections.headline: A generalist computer-use agent is defined by three per-step decisions: what to observe, how to act, and how to organize work.

sections.body: The section describes two behaviors: code execution, where the model writes one Python program combining GUI operations and shell commands, and harness-to-model decision transfer, where the model decides when to request screenshots and how to track task state. On OSWorld-v2, code execution raises Qwen3.8-Max's mean task score by 5.2 points and reduces steps per task by 17.0% against a batched GUI+CLI baseline. On-demand observation raises cache hit rate from 75.6% to 86.1% for Qwen3.8-Max and from 61.9% to 76.3% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, with higher task scores in both cases. The authors report five recurring code patterns from GPT-6 Astra runs, which illustrate uses of code rather than isolated performance gains.
sections.heading: Agent Design: Code Execution and Harness-to-Model Decision Transfer
sections.headline: Code execution and model-requested screenshots are tested on OSWorld-v2 with gains in task score and cache reuse for selected models.

sections.body: The section lists five requirements of real devices that benchmarks do not capture, including shared control with the user and windows that change during a task. The Cross-Device SDK binds each operation to an explicit device, application, window or tab. The five-layer harness prefers element-level accessibility actions, then window-targeted input, then foreground input. With one run per model on four tasks, GPT-6 Astra averages 34.5 steps and 12.9K output tokens per task, while Qwen3.8-Max averages 50.8 steps and 73.4K. Reported reasoning averages 2.6K tokens for GPT and 50.2K for Qwen. The authors state that these four tasks do not establish a general model ranking.
sections.heading: Real-Device Generalist CUA
sections.headline: On four real macOS tasks, Qwen3.8-Max averages 50.2K reasoning tokens per task against 2.6K for GPT-6 Astra under one harness.

sections.body: The roadmap says the central addition for the next release is a trained generalist computer-use model that unifies computer and browser use. Its research priorities are more efficient reasoning and execution, reliable work on users' devices, and real-device environments and benchmarks, particularly on macOS. The authors state that the current release validates agent design with existing models rather than introducing a new model. They give no delivery timeline and invite contributions to platform adapters, real-device evaluation and research goals.
sections.heading: Roadmap
sections.headline: The next release is planned to add a trained generalist computer-use model, with work on efficient reasoning and real-device benchmarks.

sections.body: The section places the work against frontier vendor systems, which the authors say leave implementation details and trajectories unavailable. It lists open GUI-centric models such as UI-TARS and OpenCUA, and hybrid systems such as CoAct-1 and UltraCUA that combine graphical control with code or tool calls. It describes the authors' earlier Qwen-UI-Agent as a unified action space with batched actions. Open harnesses such as cua and the Agent S series are described as complementary. The authors position Open Generalist CUA as coupling a trained model with a real-device harness, a cross-device SDK and execution trajectories.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Existing open computer-use models focus on graphical interfaces, while hybrid graphical-and-programmatic systems are only beginning to appear.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the design: three model decisions covering what to observe, how to act and how to organize work. Code execution lets models use intermediate results and existing programming ability, and harness-to-model decision transfer moves selected observation and task-state decisions to the model. On the offline subset, the full configuration raises mean partial score by 19.6 points and reduces steps per task by an average of 53.0% against batched GUI-only execution. The authors release code, prompts, trajectories and preliminary real-device tooling. They state that the report studies designs and introduces no newly trained model.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Across eight models, the full configuration raises mean partial score by 19.6 points on the offline OSWorld-v2 subset.

sections.body: Appendix A gives evaluation details for the 82-task offline subset of OSWorld-v2 v2.1, which excludes 26 tasks requiring Internet access, and defines task score and full-task success. Appendix B describes the four real macOS tasks: workbook reasoning, PDF form filling, shopping research and hotel comparison. Appendix C reproduces the code-execution and harness-to-model prompts, including the full OpenGCUA system prompt, with the login credential redacted. Appendix D walks through selected stages from GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 runs, each with a saved evaluator result of 1.0.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists evaluation details, real-device task descriptions, the prompts, and trajectory examples from GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.
